meta.title: Why Putin Is So Hard to Kill
meta.working_title: The Armoured Car, the Ghost Train and the Fake Offices: How Putin Stays Alive
meta.device: A red 'WHERE IS PUTIN?' pin that keeps jumping between five residences on a map of Russia. Each act adds one more layer of protection around the pin (car shell, four planes, a train line, three identical offices), and the pin never settles in one place.
meta.style: Calm, serious investigative documentary in the house 2D style, Alium character style (big-eyed, rounded cutouts as in BlackRock). Painted plates: grey Moscow highways in sleet, a snowy forest residence, a jet cabin at night, a dark green train crossing birch forest, a wood-panelled office lit by one desk lamp. Cold blues and greys with one warm accent (the red pin). SFX under the VO (engine hum, rotor wash, train clatter, clock ticks); music only at combine.
meta.source: English transcript 'Why Putin Is So Hard to Kill' (~2,200 words), rewritten in our own words, sponsor read removed, claims hedged and attributed.

shots.vo: When Putin flies abroad, reports say four identical planes take off. Only one has him on board. And that is just one of his tricks.
shots.visual: Map of Russia at night; a red pin labelled WHERE IS PUTIN? hops between five glowing points.
shots.anim: The pin blinks out and reappears at a new residence every beat.

shots.vo: An armoured car that shrugs off grenades. Four identical planes in the sky at once.
shots.visual: Split screen: a black limousine on a highway; four identical jets in a row.
shots.anim: Car rolls in on the left; four jets slide in on the right one after another.

shots.vo: A train that is on no timetable, and offices that look the same but sit hundreds of kilometres apart.
shots.visual: A dark train racing past an empty platform; three identical desks side by side.
shots.anim: Train blurs past; the three desks match up like a spot-the-difference puzzle.

shots.vo: Each one tells us something about how Russia works, and about the man at the top.
shots.visual: Silhouette of a man at a long table, lit by a single lamp.
shots.anim: Slow push in; the lamp flickers once.

shots.visual: Title over the red pin on the map.
shots.onscreen: WHY PUTIN IS SO HARD TO KILL
shots.anim: Title thuds in; the pin flickers away.

acts.name: Act 1: A Man of Many Homes

shots.vo: Since 2000, Putin has spent much of his time at Novo-Ogaryovo, a guarded estate in the forest west of Moscow.
shots.visual: Map zooms to Moscow; a pin drops on a snowy forest compound.
shots.anim: Map zooms; pin drops with a soft thud.

shots.vo: He also spends long stretches at a lakeside residence at Valdai, between Moscow and St Petersburg.
shots.visual: A wooden residence on a frozen lake, smoke from a chimney.
shots.anim: Smoke curls; snow drifts across the lake.

shots.vo: There is a summer residence at Sochi on the Black Sea, and a huge palace on the coast at Cape Idokopas that investigators link to him. He denies owning it.
shots.visual: Map slides south; two more pins drop on the Black Sea coast.
shots.anim: Two pins drop; a question mark hangs over the palace pin.

shots.vo: Having many homes is useful. But to get between them, or to meet other leaders, he has to travel.
shots.visual: A route line snakes between the pins.
shots.anim: A dotted route draws itself between the residences.

shots.vo: And a leader on the move is a leader at his most exposed.
shots.visual: The red pin on the route line pulses like a target.
shots.anim: Crosshairs fade in around the moving pin.

shots.vo: He is guarded day and night by uniformed officers and by plain-clothes agents you would never notice.
shots.visual: Bodyguards in dark coats around a car; one agent in a civilian jacket reading a newspaper nearby.
shots.anim: Guards scan left and right; the newspaper agent glances up over the page.

shots.vo: But the Kremlin's security leans on one idea above everything else: nobody should be able to predict where he will be.
shots.visual: A wall calendar with every date scribbled out.
shots.anim: Each date is crossed out in quick strokes.

shots.vo: This is his car, a Russian-built Aurus Senat limousine.
shots.visual: A long black limousine glides along a grey Moscow highway in sleet.
shots.anim: Car glides; wipers sweep; pan follows.

shots.vo: Inside it is all leather, soft seats and a small bar. Outside, it is built like a vault.
shots.visual: Cutaway of the car: plush cabin on top, thick armour plates drawn in the shell.
shots.anim: The outer skin peels back to show layered armour.

shots.vo: Picture an ambush on the road into Moscow. Attackers open fire.
shots.visual: Figures crouched behind a barrier aim at the passing car.
shots.anim: Muzzle flashes; sparks bounce off the car body.

shots.vo: The armour is designed to stop heavy rounds, reportedly even armour-piercing ones.
shots.visual: Bullets flatten against the window glass.
shots.anim: Flattened bullets drop away from the glass.

shots.vo: A grenade lands under the car. It rolls on through the smoke.
shots.visual: Smoke cloud; the car emerges from it unscratched.
shots.anim: Flash and smoke; the car drives out the other side.

shots.vo: The fuel tank is sealed against blasts, and the tyres are built to keep running even after they are shot out.
shots.visual: Diagram labels: SEALED TANK, RUN-FLAT TYRES.
shots.anim: Labels snap on with a ping each.

shots.vo: It weighs around six and a half tonnes, but a twin-turbo V8 with a hybrid system can still push it to around 160 or 170 kilometres an hour, depending on the source.
shots.visual: Speedometer needle climbing; the heavy car accelerating.
shots.anim: Needle swings up; speed lines streak.

shots.vo: The cabin can seal itself and filter the air, so a gas attack would struggle to reach the passenger. There is an emergency exit too.
shots.visual: Cabin closes; a filter fan spins; a hatch outline glows.
shots.anim: Fan spins; the escape hatch outline pulses.

shots.vo: For short trips, the car is his shield. For long ones, he takes to the air.
shots.visual: The car pulls up beside a large four-engine jet on a runway.
shots.anim: Car stops; camera tilts up to the jet.

shots.vo: His long-range jet is an Ilyushin Il-96, a four-engine airliner designed in the late Soviet years.
shots.visual: A wide-body jet climbing through cloud with four engines.
shots.anim: Jet climbs; cloud slides past.

shots.vo: By today's standards it is old. Most airlines replaced four-engine jets years ago. Russia keeps flying its own.
shots.visual: Side-by-side: a modern twin-engine jet and the Il-96 with four engines.
shots.anim: Engine counts tick up under each plane.

shots.vo: The presidential version, nicknamed the Flying Kremlin, has a bedroom, a meeting room, a dining area and, reportedly, a gym.
shots.visual: Cutaway of the plane: rooms laid out like a doll's house.
shots.anim: Each room lights up in turn from nose to tail.

shots.vo: Reports also describe a secure communications system, defences against missiles, and an escape option.
shots.visual: Labels around the jet: COMMS, MISSILE DEFENCE, ESCAPE.
shots.anim: Labels appear with radar sweeps.

shots.vo: When he flies abroad, fighter jets can escort him.
shots.visual: Two fighters slide into formation beside the big jet.
shots.anim: Fighters roll into position; engine roar.

shots.vo: Intelligence reports even say a team of personal doctors travels with him.
shots.visual: Doctors in white coats in a row of seats with medical cases.
shots.anim: Doctors open cases in unison.

shots.vo: And the jet is said to be one of four near-identical planes. When he travels, the others take off too, on different routes.
shots.visual: Four jet icons leaving Moscow along four different lines.
shots.anim: Four routes fan out; a question mark hops between them.

shots.vo: The trick has a weakness. Planes are easy to follow.
shots.visual: A laptop showing a flight-tracking map covered in plane icons.
shots.anim: Plane icons crawl across the screen.

shots.vo: Russian investigative journalist Ilya Rozhdestvensky of the Dossier Center, who works from exile, points out that public flight-tracking sites log aircraft all day long.
shots.visual: The journalist at a desk with documents and a laptop.
shots.anim: He taps a tracked plane on screen.

shots.vo: In theory, a powerful enough enemy could go after all four at once. Which may be why Putin often prefers the train.
shots.visual: Four plane icons turn red one by one; then a train whistle and a cut.
shots.anim: Plane icons flash red; a whistle blows.

shots.vo: If this train rolled past your window, you probably would not look twice. Grey carriages, red stripes, like thousands of others in Russia.
shots.visual: A grey train with red stripes crossing a birch forest.
shots.anim: Train clatters through; birch trunks flick past.

shots.vo: Look closer and a few details stand out: several diesel engines at the front, and a small dome on the roof for special communications.
shots.visual: Close-up of the locomotives and a dome on one roof, circled.
shots.anim: A red circle draws around the dome.

shots.vo: The Kremlin has shown pictures of a meeting room on board. For years, nobody outside knew what the rest looked like.
shots.visual: A neat conference table in a carriage; the rest of the train in shadow.
shots.anim: Lights on in one carriage; the others stay dark.

shots.vo: Then the Dossier Center published documents it says were leaked from inside a Russian company that builds custom railway carriages.
shots.visual: A folder stamped CONFIDENTIAL slides onto a desk; blueprints fan out.
shots.anim: Stamp thuds; blueprints spread.

shots.vo: According to those files, the carriages are armoured and so heavy that each one rides on six axles instead of the usual four.
shots.visual: Blueprint of a carriage; wheel count highlighted: 4 crossed out, 6 circled.
shots.anim: The 4 crosses out; 6 stamps in.

shots.vo: There is a sleeping car, an office car and a restaurant car.
shots.visual: Carriage by carriage: bed, desk, dining table.
shots.anim: Each carriage lights in turn as the camera tracks along.

shots.vo: The leaks also describe a gym, a soundproofed beauty salon with a massage table, and a tiled spa with a Turkish steam bath. The Kremlin denies Putin has ever used carriages like these.
shots.visual: Steam rising in a tiled room; a DENIED stamp lands over it.
shots.anim: Steam curls; the DENIED stamp lands with a thud.

shots.vo: Rozhdestvensky says the train does not appear on public timetables. Someone inside Russian Railways could see it, but an ordinary passenger never would.
shots.visual: A departures board where one line is blank.
shots.anim: Board flaps; one row stays blank.

shots.vo: It runs straight through stations without stopping.
shots.visual: The train blasts past an empty platform; papers swirl.
shots.anim: Papers swirl in the train's wake.

shots.vo: And according to the investigation, there are private stations built for him near his homes: at Bocharov Ruchey in Sochi, at Novo-Ogaryovo outside Moscow, and at Valdai, where he spends much of the year.
shots.visual: Three private platforms appear on the map next to three residence pins.
shots.anim: Track lines draw between the private stations.

shots.vo: So on any given day, it is hard to say which home he is actually in.
shots.visual: The red pin flickers between all three stations.
shots.anim: The pin blinks across the three locations.

shots.vo: Since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Putin has held many meetings by video, from what is presented as his office at Novo-Ogaryovo.
shots.visual: Putin at a desk facing a big screen of faces.
shots.anim: Faces on the screen nod; a clock ticks.

shots.vo: Russians know that room by sight: the desk, the wood panels, the flags.
shots.visual: The office from the TV angle.
shots.anim: Slow push; the lamp glows.

shots.vo: But journalists comparing the footage spotted something odd. The door handles sit at different heights.
shots.visual: Two frames side by side; door handles circled at different heights.
shots.anim: Red circles draw; a line links the two handles.

shots.vo: The thermostat moves around. The wall panels line up differently. The vents and TV stands do not match.
shots.visual: Three quick circled details: thermostat, wall panels, vents.
shots.anim: Each detail circles with a pen squeak.

shots.vo: The likely answer: near-copies of the office have been built at other residences, reportedly including Valdai and Sochi.
shots.visual: Three identical offices appear side by side on the map.
shots.anim: Three office icons pop onto the map.

shots.vo: Rozhdestvensky's reading is that the copies let him record a statement that appears to come from Novo-Ogaryovo while he is somewhere else entirely.
shots.visual: A camera crew filming; the label NOVO-OGARYOVO on screen while the map pin sits in Sochi.
shots.anim: Camera light blinks; on-screen label says one place, the map pin another.

shots.vo: If almost nobody knows where he is, it is very hard to target him.
shots.visual: The red pin dissolves into fog.
shots.anim: Fog rolls over the pin.

shots.vo: Reports also say that since the war began he has stayed away from his Sochi summer house out of fear of Ukrainian drones.
shots.visual: A coastal villa under a sky dotted with small drones.
shots.anim: Drone buzz; the villa's lights go out.

shots.vo: Where does this level of caution come from? Part of the answer may be his past. Putin was a KGB officer in East Germany.
shots.visual: 1980s Dresden street at night; a young officer in a trench coat.
shots.anim: Street lamp buzzes; snow falls.

shots.vo: He watched that state collapse in 1989 as crowds took to the streets. Many biographers think it left him deeply distrustful of crowds and uprisings.
shots.visual: Crowds with candles in the street; the young officer watches from a doorway.
shots.anim: Candles flicker; the officer steps back into shadow.

shots.vo: Today, much of his inner circle still comes from the security services.
shots.visual: A table of men in dark suits; each with a small KGB-era badge.
shots.anim: Badges glint one by one.

shots.vo: He also knows how many people want him gone: critics he has jailed, rivals, and a country he invaded.
shots.visual: Map of Ukraine and Russia with a border line; arrows of drones crossing.
shots.anim: Drone arrows pulse across the border.

shots.vo: Remember the very long tables he used during meetings in 2022? Guests sat metres away.
shots.visual: A huge white table with Putin at one end and a guest far away at the other.
shots.anim: Camera pulls back to show the full absurd length.

shots.vo: His meals are reportedly cooked by his own chefs with their own ingredients, and tested before he eats.
shots.visual: A chef in a white hat; a taster with a small test kit.
shots.anim: Pan sizzles; a test strip changes colour.

shots.vo: Reports even claim his guards collect his waste on foreign trips, so no other country can study his health.
shots.visual: A bodyguard holding a small sealed case, looking straight ahead.
shots.anim: He tightens his grip on the case. Beat.

shots.vo: The way his system works makes access to him the real currency. Rozhdestvensky says those who can reach him hold power, and those who can't hold none.
shots.visual: A pyramid of figures; light falls only on those nearest the top.
shots.anim: Light dims level by level down the pyramid.

shots.vo: Ukraine's former military intelligence chief, Kyrylo Budanov, has claimed Putin uses body doubles who have had surgery to look like him. The Kremlin denies it, and there is no public proof.
shots.visual: Three identical silhouettes in a row; a CLAIM tag over them.
shots.anim: The silhouettes blink; a 'NO PROOF' tag slides in.

shots.vo: A former officer of his protection service, Gleb Karakulov, who fled Russia in 2023, described something simpler: decoy runs.
shots.visual: A man in a plain jacket speaking to camera in a dim room.
shots.anim: Small push in as he talks.

shots.vo: A motorcade drives to a plane, someone who looks a bit like Putin climbs aboard, and the plane flies to Moscow. The real Putin stays where he is.
shots.visual: A motorcade on a runway; a lookalike walks up the steps; the plane leaves while the real man watches from a window far away.
shots.anim: The decoy waves from the steps; cut to the real man at a window.

shots.vo: So here is the system: an armoured car, four lookalike planes, a train on no timetable, three copies of the same office, and maybe a decoy or two.
shots.visual: All the layers stack around the red pin: car shell, planes, train line, offices.
shots.anim: Each layer snaps into place around the pin.

shots.vo: It may be one of the most protected lives on earth.
shots.visual: The pin glowing inside layer after layer of rings.
shots.anim: Rings of protection pulse outward.

shots.vo: And yet, for all of it, there seems to be one thing it cannot buy him: the feeling of being safe.
shots.visual: A man alone at the far end of the long table; the lamp clicks off.
shots.anim: Lamp clicks off; silence.

shots.visual: End card.
shots.onscreen: WHY PUTIN IS SO HARD TO KILL
shots.anim: Title fades over the pin.

hooks: Every time Putin flies, four identical planes take off. Only one has him on board. Here's why you'll never know which.
What if the man you see on Russian TV isn't where they say he is? Journalists checked the door handles.

fixes: Aurus Senat specs vary by source: ~6.5 t armoured, 4.4 L twin-turbo V8 hybrid; top speed given as 160-170 km/h; script hedges.
Il-96-300PU: four-engine Soviet-era design (first flight 1988). 'Four identical planes' is a media report; stated as 'said to be'.

Dossier Center (Mikhail Khodorkovsky-funded) published the train leak in 2023; company named in reports as Tver-based / 'Tsirkon Servis' contractor. Script says 'a Russian company that builds custom railway carriages'.
Kremlin denied Putin used the spa carriage; stated on screen.
Private stations: Bocharov Ruchey (Sochi), Novo-Ogaryovo, Valdai, attributed to Rozhdestvensky.
Office copies: reported by Proekt (2023) comparing footage; script says 'journalists' and 'reportedly'.
Body doubles: claim by Kyrylo Budanov (HUR chief until 2025); Kremlin denies; no public proof stated.
Gleb Karakulov: FSO officer who defected in 2023 and spoke to the Dossier Center; described decoy flights, not true doubles.
Waste-collection claim: Paris Match / French reporting (2022), stated as 'reports claim'.
Putin served in the KGB in Dresden 1985-1990.
cuts: Interview quotes paraphrased and attributed rather than quoted.
'Village torn down' near Sochi residence dropped (single unverified report).
